items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. It’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is 🫩 and that says a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first… The reality of where we currently are Technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI . I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity. It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop , somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children . The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry. The technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now . In the space between that piece being published and now , we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes . The mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume , regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either. This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least. The symptoms of where we currently are The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide , devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers . It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing. Some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. items.full: After years of uncertainty under corporate ownership, CSS-Tricks has a new chapter and a new owner. Geoff Graham joins Matt Medeiros to talk about bringing the beloved web development resource back to its community roots and building a sustainable future for the site. Geoff shares how DigitalOcean made the transition possible, why he wants CSS-Tricks… After years of uncertainty under corporate ownership, CSS-Tricks has a new chapter and a new owner. Geoff Graham joins Matt Medeiros to talk about bringing the beloved web development resource back to its community roots and building a sustainable future for the site. Geoff shares how DigitalOcean made the transition possible, why he wants CSS-Tricks to become a learning community rather than just another content site , and how memberships, sponsorships, and new educational opportunities will help support it. The conversation also gets into the bigger questions facing WordPress: Is AI making WordPress less necessary? Does the platform need a lighter version for simpler sites? And as AI changes how developers work, why will human expertise, education, and community matter even more? Plus, Geoff explains why CSS-Tricks is embracing multiple revenue streams, experimenting with cohort-based learning, and focusing on engagement over page views. New articles and episodes, plus the week’s WordPress news. A five-minute read. Free.

items.title: Discover 2WayMicropay: Sell WordPress Content From One Cent and Give Readers Credits to Spend
items.desc: Most readers won't subscribe for one article, and most micropayment systems still ask them to fund a wallet first. 2WayMicropay lets WordPress publishers charge from one cent and hand readers credits to spend on that content. The post " Discover 2WayMicropay: Sell WordPress Content From One Cent and Give Readers Credits to Spend " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: A visitor lands on one of your best articles from search, reads the opening, and hits a subscription wall. They wanted that one piece, not a monthly plan, so they leave, even though they’d probably have paid a dollar for it. Micropayments were supposed to close that gap, but most systems still ask a stranger to sign up and fund a wallet before they’ve read anything worth paying for. 2WayMicropay , from Qixit, removes that step by letting publishers charge from one cent and also hand readers credits to spend. The quickest way to see what’s different is to go through the flow as a reader. Qixit’s interactive paywall demo has you create a free Qixit consumer account, receive complimentary credits, and spend them to unlock premium articles about how 2WayMicropay works. Notice the order of events. You’re asked for an account, but never for a deposit, because the credits you spend arrive through the same system that charges for the content. Qixit is the company and account platform, and 2WayMicropay is its two-way micropayment product. The 2WayMicropay WordPress plugin lets visitors pay for posts, pages, comments, video, audio, downloads and other content in Qix Credits, at prices from one cent up to several dollars. The “two-way” part is what sets it apart. Most payment systems only move value from customer to seller, while 2WayMicropay also lets publishers, advertisers and sponsors send credits to visitors, which readers can then spend on content from participating publishers. It’s worth knowing that Qix Credits are platform credits. Qixit is clear that they aren’t cash or legal tender, and that redemption and withdrawal follow its own agreements and policies. You don’t have to drop subscriptions, memberships or ads to use it. 2WayMicropay sits beside them as an à-la-carte option for the readers a subscription wall turns away. Our guide to ways to monetize WordPress covers how the other models fit together. Checkout is hosted by Qixit, so there’s nothing for you to build. A visitor signs in or creates a free Qixit account, confirms the purchase, and gets access once payment goes through. The plugin is also a showcase for a broader platform. Qixit’s vendor tools and developer API let teams add the same purchase and payout links to custom websites and other applications. Each premium item gets an access rule: pay once and view forever, pay per view, limited hours, or session only. For a free preview, you add a WordPress “More” break and enable “Use Pay-per-play works the same way for video, audio and games through a product shortcode. That lets podcasters and video creators charge for a single episode on their own site. Payout links are created in Qixit’s vendor portal and added to posts with a shortcode or URL. For each one you set the amount, the credit type, a destination URL, a total budget and an optional expiry date. Qix Credits work across participating sites, while site-specific promotional credits can only be spent on your content, which gives readers a reason to come back. Either type can fund free trials or reward readers for viewing a sponsor’s page, completing a survey or referring a friend. You don’t need to open each post to monetize

items.full: I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) items.title: scroll-state()
items.desc: The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. scroll-state() originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. Far from doom, that’s pretty neat-o speedo. (Okay, you’re right, there’s nothing neat-o about a speedo). You can do lots of things that used to require JavaScript, like revealing the navigation when a user scrolls up or animating in a back to top link once the user scrolls down. While scroll-state() , with those slimming parentheses, looks like a function, it’s not technically one. It’s a container query ( @container ) like style() . Since scroll-state() is a query, the website is basically asking the browser whether a particular feature of a container has a specific value. If it does, the styles within the brackets will apply. If it doesn’t have that feature at all or has the feature, but the value is different, the @container query is false and the styles in the brackets will not apply. In the following demo (which we’ll dissect in a bit), a “Back to Top” link slides in from the bottom as you scroll down the page. Syntax @container scroll-state( <scroll-state-feature>: <value> ) { /* styles */ } Values scroll-state() has four possible features and each of those has a variety of possible values. scrolled Asks if a container has been scrolled in a given direction: scrollable Asks if a container can be scrolled in a given direction: stuck Asks if a sticky-positioned element is stuck: snapped Asks if a snap target has been snapped on a particular axis: Demos Scrolled First let’s look at the scrolled feature. This is the demo we saw at the beginning where we animate a back-to-top link when we scroll down: .toplink { position: fixed; bottom: 0.125em; right: 1em; translate: 0 200px; transition: translate 0.5s; @container top-revealer scroll-state(scrolled: block-end) { translate: 0 0; transition: translate 0.5s; } } When the scroll container is scrolled toward the block-end (downward in this case) the translate applies and the .toplink element animates up into the visible area. Because we’re using a transition , when we scroll a different direction (up and down/ block-start and block-end are the only options here), it nicely animates out. Scrollable While the scrolling direction in the demo above is pretty clear, what if this page was translated into a different language? Or we had a hero image that covered the entire viewport? One way we could indicate the scroll direction would be to have an arrow or other signifier animating and pointing in the correct direction. (I’m more a believer in constructing your page such that scroll direction is pretty obvious; however, I can foresee situations where an indicator was the best user experience or where translations/writing-mode changes could obscure what scrolling direction was appropriate.) .scrollindicator { display: none; @container top-revealer scroll-state(scrollable: block-end) { display: block; } } One nice thing about the scrollable feature is that when you scroll to the end of the scrollable area, it shuts off.
